/photos/HST/_DSC0054-Edit.jpg.title: Starlight on the Slabs
/photos/HST/_DSC0054-Edit.jpg.alt: Creek running over granite slabs in the Big Arroyo beneath a deep blue star-lit sky, Sequoia National Park.
/photos/HST/_DSC0054-Edit.jpg.story: This one took hours and three separate takes — a golden hour version, a blue hour version, and an astro version once it was properly dark. What survived is a time blend: the sky from the astro frame, the foreground and middle ground from blue hour, thirteen seconds at ISO 80 while there was still light enough to hold texture in the granite. Shoot the stars alone and the bottom half of the picture is just black.
/photos/HST/_DSC0054-Edit.jpg.location: Big Arroyo, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC0181.jpg.title: Waiting Out the Weather
/photos/HST/_DSC0181.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of two backpackers beside Guitar Lake below Mount Whitney with storm cloud building above.
/photos/HST/_DSC0181.jpg.story: Storm light is the one gift of a Sierra afternoon in July — hard directional sun beneath a heavy lid, and gone within minutes. Seventy millimetres compresses the cloud down onto the basin, and the two figures stay tiny at the waterline because that is the honest proportion of the place. Monochrome: the cloud had all of the drama and none of the colour worth keeping.
/photos/HST/_DSC0181.jpg.location: Guitar Lake, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC0221.jpg.title: Lenticulars at First Light
/photos/HST/_DSC0221.jpg.alt: Lenticular clouds over the Sierra crest at dawn, seen from high on Mount Whitney above the Great Western Divide.
/photos/HST/_DSC0221.jpg.story: The colour before sunrise is the good material up here — cool, soft, and finished the instant direct light touches the ridges. Lenticulars mean serious wind aloft, which is bad news for a climb and excellent news for a photograph. Sixty-three millimetres tightened it to the layers I wanted: dark ridge across the bottom, the crest still in shadow, and the whole sky working above it.

/photos/HST/_DSC0238-Edit.jpg.title: Rothko's Sierra
/photos/HST/_DSC0238-Edit.jpg.alt: Pink dawn light on snow-streaked Sierra peaks photographed at 172mm from high on Mount Whitney, California.
/photos/HST/_DSC0238-Edit.jpg.story: The title is the idea. At 172mm the ridges stop reading as mountains and become horizontal bands of colour stacked one on the next — about as close to a colour field as landscape photography gets. Long lenses do exactly that: they flatten distance into layers. Handheld at ISO 1000 and 1/640, because at that hour and that temperature a tripod was never going to happen.

/photos/HST/_DSC0263-Edit.jpg.title: Sunrise Through the Windows
/photos/HST/_DSC0263-Edit.jpg.alt: Sunrise rays through a granite window on the Mount Whitney Trail, looking east over the Owens Valley.
/photos/HST/_DSC0263-Edit.jpg.story: Shooting into a rising sun is normally how you make a bad photograph. The exception is enough haze in the air to turn the light into visible shafts, and there was a valley full of it. The granite does two jobs — it frames the opening, and it gives the lens something dark to sit against, which keeps flare manageable. Metered for the sky and let the rock fall to silhouette.

/photos/HST/_DSC0293.jpg.title: Down from Trail Crest
/photos/HST/_DSC0293.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of two hikers descending the switchbacks below Trail Crest above a lake, Mount Whitney.
/photos/HST/_DSC0293.jpg.story: Early side light down a long slope is the best thing that can happen to a mountain: it separates each ridge from the next and puts texture into ground that reads flat by noon. The two figures set the scale of the switchbacks — without them this is an abstract. Black and white because the low sun had already gone warm, and the warmth was pulling attention off the structure.

/photos/HST/_DSC9760-HDR-Edit.jpg.title: Arnica Under the Spires
/photos/HST/_DSC9760-HDR-Edit.jpg.alt: Yellow arnica flowers on granite below the spires of Rowell Tower and Serpent's Tooth, Hamilton Lakes, Sequoia.
/photos/HST/_DSC9760-HDR-Edit.jpg.story: A near-far composition lives or dies on how close you are willing to get. The 14mm went down almost into the arnica — close enough that depth of field became the whole problem, solved at f/11 with the focus set a third of the way in. The range between shaded petals and sunlit granite needed a bracket. Cloud did the rest; in clear midday light there is no picture here.
/photos/HST/_DSC9760-HDR-Edit.jpg.location: Hamilton Lakes, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC9765-HDR.jpg.title: Lower Hamilton
/photos/HST/_DSC9765-HDR.jpg.alt: Lower Hamilton Lake in a bowl of polished granite on the High Sierra Trail, Sequoia National Park, under building cloud.
/photos/HST/_DSC9765-HDR.jpg.story: Twenty past twelve is the hour most landscape photographers are asleep or eating, and usually they are right. Moving cloud saved it — every few minutes the sun went behind, the granite stopped blowing out and the pool turned from glare to green. I bracketed and waited for those windows. The rock handles the composition on its own here: the trail climbs in the same lines the water falls.
/photos/HST/_DSC9765-HDR.jpg.location: Hamilton Lakes, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC9825-Edit.jpg.title: Thirty Seconds
/photos/HST/_DSC9825-Edit.jpg.alt: Long exposure of Hamilton Lake at dusk with a bleached driftwood log in the foreground, Sequoia National Park.
/photos/HST/_DSC9825-Edit.jpg.story: I worked this one for an entire evening, waiting on cloud that would actually do something. The log was the reason to be there — bleached, half-sunk, pointing straight into the frame — so the tripod went into the water beside it and the 14mm went low. Thirty seconds at f/11 turned the surface to slate. The range between the bright sky and the shaded wood was well past what a single frame holds, so it is a blend of brackets.
/photos/HST/_DSC9825-Edit.jpg.location: Hamilton Lakes, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC9860.jpg.title: The Climb Out of Hamilton
/photos/HST/_DSC9860.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of a hiker on the blasted ledge trail cut into the headwall above Hamilton Lake, Sequoia.
/photos/HST/_DSC9860.jpg.story: Scale is the hardest thing to photograph in this range and the only dependable solution is a person. So the frame is built to be mostly wall, with the figure small, high, and standing in the one patch of light on the ledge. Black and white because the rock was already doing everything — in colour it is grey stone under a blue lid, and the eye has nowhere to go.
/photos/HST/_DSC9860.jpg.location: Hamilton Lakes, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC9957.jpg.title: The Life Of a Foxtail
/photos/HST/_DSC9957.jpg.alt: Backlit foxtail pine growing out of granite in the Big Arroyo, Sequoia National Park, photographed at 500mm.
/photos/HST/_DSC9957.jpg.story: Late sun raked the tree from behind, lighting the needles while the rock stayed in shadow — a separation that lasts about twenty minutes a day. At 500mm from across the basin the background compresses to a flat wash and everything competing simply falls outside the frame. Backlight at that focal length is unforgiving about flare, so I shaded the front element by hood and shot into it anyway.
/photos/HST/_DSC9957.jpg.location: Big Arroyo, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC9970.jpg.title: Glaciated Ground
/photos/HST/_DSC9970.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of glacier-polished granite slabs and peaks in the Big Arroyo, Sequoia National Park.
/photos/HST/_DSC9970.jpg.story: A flat grey afternoon over bare, glacier-scoured rock — in colour it is worth nothing at all. Monochrome turns the slabs structural: fracture lines become leading lines, and the separation between polished stone and shadowed cracks carries what colour could not. I set the horizon high and gave the foreground two thirds of the frame, because here the ground is the subject and the peaks are only the backstop.
/photos/HST/_DSC9970.jpg.location: Big Arroyo, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/cities/_DSC5344.jpg.title: Enshrined Forever
/photos/cities/_DSC5344.jpg.alt: Long-exposure black-and-white photo of the Lincoln Memorial statue with constantly passing visitors
/photos/cities/_DSC5344.jpg.story: I set up inside the chamber, and with everyone too busy to notice me, I had time to work the shot. People streamed past the whole time, while Lincoln has sat there for decades — that contrast, the still monument against the flowing crowd, was the whole idea. I held a five-second exposure so the visitors blurred into ghosts while the statue stayed perfectly sharp.

/photos/cities/_DSC8037.jpg.title: Pacific Park After Dark
/photos/cities/_DSC8037.jpg.alt: Long-exposure night photo of Santa Monica Pier's lit Ferris wheel and roller coaster reflected on the wet beach.
/photos/cities/_DSC8037.jpg.story: I walked down onto the sand well after sunset, when the Pacific Wheel and the little roller coaster were the brightest things for miles. The idea was to let the tide do the work: a four-second exposure smeared the incoming surf into a soft sheen and stretched every pink and purple light into long ribbons across the wet beach. At f/8 the pier stayed crisp while the water turned to glass.
/photos/cities/_DSC8037.jpg.location: Santa Monica Pier, Santa Monica, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC5570.jpg.title: Bloom and Basin
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5570.jpg.alt: Desert gold wildflowers on a slope above the salt flats of Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5570.jpg.story: I made this on the way up rather than at the top. From down on the flat the two things never meet, but from the slope the flowers stack into verticals and the basin lays a hard horizontal in behind them, warm against cool. That is the entire picture. I kept the bloom close enough to the lens that it reads as texture instead of as a subject.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5570.jpg.location: Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC5599-Edit.jpg.title: False Frost
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5599-Edit.jpg.alt: Salt crust at Badwater Basin lit low across its ridges during blue hour, Death Valley National Park.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5599-Edit.jpg.story: One of my favourites, and the only frame here that isn't natural light. The camera went as low on the tripod as it would go — salt has no shape at all from standing height. Then a flash off the camera entirely, held out to one side, so the light rakes across the crust instead of flattening it. Blue hour gave me the sky; the flash gave the ground its edges.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5599-Edit.jpg.location: Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC5707.jpg.title: For Scale
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5707.jpg.alt: A lone figure silhouetted on a badlands ridge at sunrise under a pink and purple sky, Zabriskie Point, Death Valley.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5707.jpg.story: I was still hunting for a composition when someone walked up onto that hill. Everything I had tried until then failed for the same reason — nothing in the frame told you how big any of it was. They fixed that by existing. I shot it and walked away convinced I had come back with nothing, which turns out to be the least reliable feeling in photography.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5707.jpg.location: Zabriskie Point, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC5808.jpg.title: Wrong Colours
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5808.jpg.alt: Hikers on a ridge above the coloured badlands of Golden Canyon with the Panamint Range beyond, Death Valley.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5808.jpg.story: This is not the desert people picture, and it is not the mountains people picture either. The colours are wrong for both, which is exactly why I wanted it. The hikers on the ridge are walking out of the frame rather than into it, and that felt more honest about the scale of the place — you don't arrive somewhere like this, you cross it and keep going.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5808.jpg.location: Golden Canyon, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC5828.jpg.title: The Committee
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5828.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of four hikers silhouetted on the ridge of a dune at Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes, Death Valley.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5828.jpg.story: I was out scouting for sunset when this arranged itself above me: four people on the ridge, mid-argument about whether to keep climbing. One pointing, one very obviously finished. It reads like a single panel of a comic. I framed wide and let the dune take most of the picture, because the joke only works while they are still small enough to be figures rather than people.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5828.jpg.location: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC5865.jpg.title: Sand to Sky
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5865.jpg.alt: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes at blue hour, warm sand giving way to blue and pink sky over the distant salt basin.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5865.jpg.story: Sand holds the last of the warm light for a while after the sky above it has gone cold. That mismatch is the picture — a gradient running the full height of the frame, yellow at your feet, then blue, then pink out over the far basin. I composed around the transition itself rather than around any particular dune, which is why nothing here is the subject.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5865.jpg.location: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC6007.jpg.title: Fallen Sky
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6007.jpg.alt: Clouds reflected in floodwater on the salt flats of Badwater Basin, the Panamint Range beyond, Death Valley.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6007.jpg.story: Second day of trying to make something work down here. The water changed it — a flooded basin stops being ground and becomes a mirror, and once the sky is underneath you as well as above you the whole thing goes abstract. The mountains end up as the only element still reading as itself. Everything else in the frame is cloud, twice over.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6007.jpg.location: Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC6068.jpg.title: Telescope Blue
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6068.jpg.alt: Telescope Peak above Badwater Basin at late blue hour, salt formations visible beneath standing water, Death Valley.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6068.jpg.story: Late blue hour, and salt does something strange with it. White crust throws back almost everything that lands on it, so the colour of the sky ends up spread across the entire basin instead of staying up where it belongs. Telescope Peak anchors the far side. The salt formations still readable under the water are what keep this from tipping over into looking invented.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6068.jpg.location: Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC6099.jpg.title: Badwater Fire
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6099.jpg.alt: Stacked plates of salt crust leading toward a magenta sunset over Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6099.jpg.story: I was back at the car with the bag packed when the light turned, and there is no version of that where you just drive away. Everything came out again. What made the unpacking worth it was the salt — those big stacked plates run in the same direction as the clouds, so the ground and the sky pull the eye the same way instead of fighting each other.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6099.jpg.location: Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC6135.jpg.title: Soft Geometry
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6135.jpg.alt: Low-contrast sunrise over the ridges of Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes, Death Valley National Park.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6135.jpg.story: Sunrise, but barely — the contrast never really arrived, and that turned out to be the mood worth keeping. One dune low in the frame, a second behind it, and a cloud above running the other way, so the eye zigzags up through the picture. There is almost no tonal separation anywhere in it. This one holds together on shape alone, which is rarer than good light.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6135.jpg.location: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6639.jpg.title: The Sheer Scale of It
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6639.jpg.alt: The Grand Canyon seen from Pima Point, a shaft of sunlight on red buttes above the distant Colorado River.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6639.jpg.story: This was one of the first scenes the Grand Canyon showed me. What pulled me in was a single streak of light raking across the buttes and reflecting off the Colorado far below. That warm rock against the cool, hazy blue was the shot.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6767.jpg.title: The Day's Last Ember
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6767.jpg.alt: The Grand Canyon at blue hour from Mojave Point, last light on the red buttes fading into cool twilight.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6767.jpg.story: Blue hour on my first evening in the canyon. I'd waited all day at Mojave Point for exactly this light - and then the last shuttle honked for me. I fired the shutter, ran over to ask the driver for two minutes to pack, and grabbed a few more frames while I had them. Each was an 8-second exposure at f/11, so every shot felt like forever in the fading light. I had no idea I'd just made one of my favorite Grand Canyon photographs.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6792.jpg.title: The Sentinel
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6792.jpg.alt: A lone juniper at the rim of the Grand Canyon at sunrise, first light striking the cliffs at Moran Point.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6792.jpg.story: I'd planned to shoot Lipan Point that morning, but I left too late - the sun was already breaking the horizon as I drove. Rather than gamble on making it, I pulled into the first overlook, Moran Point, and started hunting for a composition. Another photographer there was working a telephoto; I wanted to go wide. I found this lone juniper clinging to the edge and waited for the light to reach it.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6882.jpg.title: An Island of Light
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6882.jpg.alt: Sunlight on Berry Butte, rising from the hazy blue ridges of the Grand Canyon at Grandview Point.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6882.jpg.story: I was scouting a sunset composition at Grandview Point when streaks of light began falling across Berry Butte, while the ridges behind it dissolved into haze. The depth was already there - I just had to isolate it. I reached for 64mm to compress the layers and let the lit rock separate from the cool, hazy background. Sometimes the canyon hands you the shot; you just have to recognize it and frame it.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6909.jpg.title: Where the Sun Pours In
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6909.jpg.alt: A wide golden-hour view of the Grand Canyon from Grandview Point, the low sun glowing through haze above a dead tree.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6909.jpg.story: Once I'd found the right spot at Grandview Point, I wanted to keep it simple — a wide, near-panoramic frame with the low golden-hour sun pouring straight through the canyon. I used this lone dead tree to anchor the middle of the composition and shot into the light at 20mm, stopping down to f/11 so the sun held a clean shape. Some frames are less about a story and more about being there when the light is this good.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6976.jpg.title: Where Ridges Dissolve
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6976.jpg.alt: Layered ridgelines of the Grand Canyon fading into morning haze, with O'Neill Butte seen from Hopi Point at sunrise.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6976.jpg.story: I stopped at Hopi Point on a morning hike to catch the sun coming up over O'Neill Butte. The light was doing the thing I love - stacking the ridgelines into receding layers as the haze separated each one. I reached for 77mm to compress those layers and let the butte sit as the anchor among them. It's a quiet, almost abstract way to photograph a place most people shoot wide.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7101.jpg.title: First light below the rim
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7101.jpg.alt: Warm morning light on a canyon wall seen from Coconino Overlook on the North Kaibab Trail
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7101.jpg.story: This was my first stop on the rim-to-rim journey I'd been wanting to do. I waited an hour for first light to come into the canyon as the clouds rolled in.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7356.jpg.title: Before the Sky Broke
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7356.jpg.alt: Wide-angle long-exposure view of Split Rock Falls, with storm clouds streaking across the sky above the canyon walls.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7356.jpg.story: After reaching Cottonwood Camp I doubled back toward the Manzanita rest area, where a small thunderstorm was rolling in. It felt like the perfect chance for a long exposure — something to play the falling water against the fast-moving clouds.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7356.jpg.location: Split Rock Falls, Grand Canyon, AZ

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7438.jpg.title: Desert's Garden
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7438.jpg.alt: A view from inside the alcove behind Ribbon Falls, a moss-covered rock in the foreground framed by the cave mouth.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7438.jpg.story: After a long day of hiking, I decided to visit Ribbon Falls. Getting the shot meant climbing up into a small alcove with all my gear, but it was worth it — sitting near the waterfall was refreshing on such a hot day. To handle the enormous dynamic range, from the shaded alcove to the bright canyon beyond, I blended two exposures together.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7592.jpg.title: Leaving the River Behind
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7592.jpg.alt: A barrel cactus in the foreground above the Colorado River, with the Black Bridge and soft evening light on the canyon walls.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7592.jpg.story: On my last evening in the canyon, I decided to photograph the Colorado River — this shot almost felt like the place saying goodbye to me. Once the light turned soft, I chose this barrel cactus to be the hero of the frame. To keep everything sharp from the spines at my feet to the bridge in the distance, I focus-stacked several frames together. Everything came together at once: the color in the river, the bridge, the light on the canyon walls, and its reflection in the water.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7696.jpg.title: An Older Rhythm of the Canyon
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7696.jpg.alt: Black-and-white photo of a mule pack train backlit by the rising sun on the South Kaibab Trail
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7696.jpg.story: While climbing back up to the South Rim, I had to stop and wait for a big mule train heading down to Phantom Ranch. I took the chance to photograph them against the canyon with the morning sun rising behind them. I shot straight into the low light and let the scene fall toward silhouette, working it in black and white so the long shadows became part of the frame.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7748.jpg.title: Light Letting Go
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7748.jpg.alt: Telephoto view of layered Grand Canyon ridgelines receding into golden sunset haze, seen from Desert View.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7748.jpg.story: On my last sunset in the park, I wanted to photograph the canyon from one of the South Rim's iconic spots, Desert View. I reached for my telephoto lens and found this almost abstract composition — the golden-hour light gradually giving out from the top of the frame to the bottom, the ridges flattening into one another the longer I looked.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7793.jpg.title: Purple Gold
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7793.jpg.alt: Wide view from Desert View, last light catching the far rim beneath a purple sky.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7793.jpg.story: As the sun had almost disappeared, I caught this last light hitting the far rim and its final reflections on the Colorado River. I waited until the sun was nearly gone so the sky would shift into that band of purple above the warm rim. The purple-and-gold contrast, set against the green trees in the foreground, makes this one of my favorite shots from the whole Grand Canyon trip.

/photos/landscapes/_DSC8109-Edit.jpg.title: Light in the Hollow
/photos/landscapes/_DSC8109-Edit.jpg.alt: Early-morning light streaming through the sea cave at El Matador Beach, god rays catching in the fog above a low-tide shoreline.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC8109-Edit.jpg.story: I planned this around the conditions — a low tide to expose El Matador's famous sea cave, and fog so the first light would hang in the air as visible streaks. The dynamic range was brutal, the bright cave mouth against the dark rock, so I blended two exposures to hold it all.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC8109-Edit.jpg.location: El Matador State Beach, Malibu, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8357-Edit.jp.title: Her Last Mile
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8357-Edit.jp.alt: Black and white photo of a lone hiker on the steep cinder slope of Cinder Cone, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8357-Edit.jp.story: She stopped to talk to my girlfriend and me while I was setting up for sunset — her last day in the park, Lassen Peak the day before. Then she walked on and became the thing the frame had been missing: something to hold that slope to scale. The conversion to black and white came later. Colour was doing nothing here that the shape of the cone wasn't already doing better.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8357-Edit.jp.location: Cinder Cone, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8392.jpg.title: Black Grit
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8392.jpg.alt: Black and white view across the crater rim of Cinder Cone, its cinder slopes curving away, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8392.jpg.story: The first volcano I ever climbed. Neither of us had seen anything like it — a cone of loose black grit with a crater bitten out of the top, and a trail that takes back half a step for every one you give it. I photographed the rim as geometry rather than as a place, and pulled the colour out afterwards. There was hardly any there to lose.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8392.jpg.location: Cinder Cone, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8413-Edit.jp.title: The Lone Guardian
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8413-Edit.jp.alt: A lone pine on the oxidised orange and black ash of the Painted Dunes at sunset, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8413-Edit.jp.story: I gave this an entire evening. The dunes only separate into bands when the sun is low enough to rake across them, and the window where the light held on this one tree — and not on the fifty others around it — lasted about two minutes. The rest of the evening was spent standing still, working out where I needed to be when it happened.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8413-Edit.jp.location: Painted Dunes, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8450-Edit.jp.title: Moon Over Sunrise
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8450-Edit.jp.alt: Full moon rising over Sunrise Peak at twilight, seen from the cinder slopes of Cinder Cone, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8450-Edit.jp.story: Entirely unplanned. We were already walking back down when the moon came up over Sunrise Peak, and I have never unpacked a tripod that fast — a full moon climbs a ridgeline quicker than feels reasonable, and every second of fumbling costs you the alignment. A single exposure: the twilight was still bright enough to hold the land and the moon in one frame.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8450-Edit.jp.location: Cinder Cone, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8632-HDR-Edi.title: Steel Clouds
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8632-HDR-Edi.alt: Kings Creek winding through a wildflower meadow below Reading Peak under heavy storm cloud, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8632-HDR-Edi.story: This was meant to be a scouting drive, but those steel-coloured clouds were not going to wait for a better-planned day. The composition needed the camera low and close to the bend, which meant standing in snowmelt at 14mm — cold enough that I stopped feeling my feet. Six stops of ND took it to a tenth of a second: enough to smooth the current without erasing it.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8632-HDR-Edi.location: Kings Creek Meadow, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8756-Edit.jp.title: Twilight Ghost
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8756-Edit.jp.alt: Full moon beside alpenglow on Lassen Peak, reflected in the still water of Manzanita Lake, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8756-Edit.jp.story: Four or five hours at this lake, shooting from golden hour through to full dark. The last hour was the hard part — cold, both of us ready to leave, waiting on the moon to clear Lassen Peak. The real obstacle was ducks. The lake was full of them, and a reflection like this needs a stretch of genuinely undisturbed water. Blended from two frames taken minutes apart.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8756-Edit.jp.location: Manzanita Lake, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8791-Edit.jp.title: Alien Grounds
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8791-Edit.jp.alt: Turquoise and milky-white hydrothermal pools and a dark mud pot in the crust at Bumpass Hell, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8791-Edit.jp.story: My first time anywhere like this. The smell reaches you before the view does, and then the colours arrive all at once — turquoise, rust, chalk-white, all within a few feet of each other. I didn't want a picture that explained where it was. I wanted the version that reads like a surface photographed from orbit, so I framed out the sky, the boardwalk and every other clue to scale.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8791-Edit.jp.location: Bumpass Hell, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8970-Edit.jp.title: Through the Trunks
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8970-Edit.jp.alt: Sunrise light on Manzanita Lake seen through pine trunks from the campground, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8970-Edit.jp.story: I was walking in to camp when I caught the light coming off the water between the trunks, with insects working in it further out. It is a photograph about backlight and nothing else — the trees are only there to break the glare into something the eye can rest on. I shot it from where I was standing. Stepping forward would have closed the gaps and cost me the whole thing.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8970-Edit.jp.location: Manzanita Lake, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC9002-HDR-Edi.title: Sunrise in Hell
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC9002-HDR-Edi.alt: Sunrise light catching steam from the fumaroles of Bumpass Hell, framed by mountain hemlock, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC9002-HDR-Edi.story: I scouted this the previous day and came back for it early. Cold air is the whole trick — the colder the morning, the more the vents give you, and at sunrise there was several times the steam I had seen in the middle of the day. The hemlocks were the other half of it. Without something solid in the corners, steam has nothing to be measured against.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC9002-HDR-Edi.location: Bumpass Hell, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/people/81dJdwzh6qQ.jpg.title: The Calm in the Glare
/photos/people/81dJdwzh6qQ.jpg.alt: studio portrait, foil backdrop, colored lighting, fashion portrait, Izhevsk
/photos/people/81dJdwzh6qQ.jpg.story: I made this studio portrait of a friend in Izhevsk, Russia. The whole image is built on contrast — colored light raking across both her face and the crumpled foil behind her, and her smooth skin set against the hard, wrinkled metal. I gelled the lights warm and magenta so the foil would catch and throw color rather than sit flat.
